paragraph.text: N10. "Sentientists are against preserving species and biodiversity"

the sentientist answer is "it depends on how this affects the animals". Species and biodiversity don't feel; individuals do. So the sentientist supports preservation when it is good for sentient beings, which is often, and questions it when it harms them, as in the mass killing of "invasive" animals. That isn't being in favor of biodiversity loss. It is refusing to treat biodiversity as a value above those who live within it, something no one does when the ones affected are human.
N. Wild animals, new minds and the future ·
DIR

this family takes the sentience criterion beyond exploitation. Many vegans disagree with parts of it, and the debate is legitimate. The test proposed in each chapter is simple: apply the same scenario to human beings and see whether the answer would be accepted; if it would not, that shows speciesism.
1. Formulation
"You don't care whether a species goes extinct. Sentientists only think about the individual animal, and nature can go hang."
Sentientism says that only beings capable of feeling matter morally in themselves.
Species, ecosystems and biodiversity don't feel.
So, for the sentientist, species and biodiversity have no value.
Anyone who sees no value in biodiversity is against preserving it, or indifferent to its loss.
So sentientists are against preserving species and biodiversity.

P1 and P2 are correct. The error lies in P3, which confuses "having no value in itself" with "having no value at all", and in P4, which confuses "not being the supreme value" with "being something to fight".
The argument is
: from "biodiversity isn't an end in itself" it doesn't follow that "biodiversity doesn't matter".

3. Answer for children

A forest doesn't feel pain, but the animals who live in it do. So when someone wants to protect the forest, we ask: is this good for the animals who live there? Almost always it is, and then we help. But if, to "protect" the forest, someone wants to kill lots of animals, we ask them to look for another way. Caring about animals one by one isn't being against the forest.
4. Short answer

I'm not against preservation. I just ask who the preservation is good for. A species feels nothing; its animals do. When protecting a habitat prevents hunger, fire and death, I support it, and that's the most common case. When "preserving" means killing millions of animals because they were born in the wrong place, I question it. It's the same with people: we value the diversity of cultures, but not at the cost of people's suffering.
"Would you accept preserving a human culture by forcing its members to suffer in order to keep it going? If not, why does the rule change when they're animals?"
5. Full answer
(a) Reconstruction and diagnosis
The phrase assumes there are only two possible positions. There are at least three:
Position
What it says about biodiversity
Who holds it
Supreme value
It must be preserved even at the cost of the suffering and death of individuals
Part of environmental ethics and conservation practice
Value for those who feel
It matters a great deal, to the extent that it affects sentient beings
Sentientism
No value
It makes no difference whether it is lost
The position attributed to sentientists
The argument assigns sentientists to the third row, when they are in the second.
(b) Where the argument breaks

text.bold: 1. Having no value in itself isn't having no value.

paragraph.text: Public health, peace and clean water don't feel anything either, and no one concludes that they don't matter. They matter a great deal, because of what they mean for those who feel. The same goes for habitats and for the variety of life forms.

text.bold: 2. Most of the time, the goals coincide.

paragraph.text: Habitat loss and ecological collapse cause suffering and death on a huge scale: WWF estimated that nearly 3 billion animals were killed or displaced by the Australian bushfires of 2019 and 2020. And the main cause of biodiversity loss in the world is the food system: according to a report by the British institute Chatham House, supported by the UN Environment Programme, agriculture is the identified threat to 24,000 of the 28,000 species assessed as at risk of extinction, and one of the ways out it points to is a more plant-based diet. The main practical demand of those who defend sentient beings, the end of animal farming, is also one of the measures most favorable to biodiversity.

text.bold: 3. The conflict appears in the method.

paragraph.text: The sentientist questions preservation when it is carried out against the animals. Three examples: the mass killing of "invasive" animals (in 2015 the Australian government set a target of killing 2 million feral cats in five years, and an estimated 1.5 million were killed); the reintroduction of predators without anyone assessing what it means for the animals who will be hunted; and captive breeding programs that keep individuals confined for life in the name of the species (I12). N3 covers these programs in more detail.

We value the diversity of cultures, languages and peoples. Even so, no one accepts preserving a culture by forbidding its members to leave it, to receive medical care or to change their lives, and no one would accept eliminating "outsiders" to maintain an "original" population. When the ones affected are human, diversity is valued for what it means to people, never above them. The sentientist simply applies the same rule to the other beings who feel.

text.bold: 5. "So you don't care if a species goes extinct?" Not so.

paragraph.text: Extinctions almost always happen through hunger, hunting, disease and habitat destruction, which are harms to individuals, and they can affect many other sentient beings, including people who care about that species. What the sentientist denies is that there is, on top of all this, a harm to the species as if it were someone (A10).

text.bold: 6. The proposal is to study wellbeing, not to abandon ecology.

paragraph.text: In 1995 the economist Yew-Kwang Ng proposed welfare biology: the study of living things and their environment with respect to their welfare. In the same paper, Ng used an evolutionary model to suggest that suffering probably outweighs wellbeing in nature. In 2019, he and Zach Groff found an error in that model and concluded that, once corrected, it doesn't tell us which predominates; and Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) argue that wild animals' lives may be far more positive than is assumed. The question of the balance remains open, which is one more reason for the research the field proposes. Catia Faria and Oscar Horta describe it as the study of the circumstances that affect wild animals' wellbeing and of how to carry out safe, feasible interventions to help them. Unlike ecology and conservation biology, which treat animals as parts of populations and ecosystems, it looks at each individual. Faced with a conservation measure, the question is no longer only whether it preserves the species or the ecosystem, but also how it affects the wellbeing of each animal it reaches, comparing the alternatives by that criterion. Organizations such as Animal Ethics and Wild Animal Initiative work for that study to exist in universities. The latter states that "identifying more humane ways to control populations has great potential to improve the lives of many wild animals". It's a research agenda that adds one question to conservation: how are the individuals doing?
In the book
(Reasons to Help, 2022, pp. 176–177), the philosopher Luciano Carlos Cunha separates three families of environmentalist views:
, which gives value in themselves to wholes such as species and ecosystems (ecocentrism is one variant);
, which values what has a non-human origin, or has been little altered by humans; and
, which gives value to each living organism, sentient or not. The accusation usually assumes they all condemn the same thing, but their demands are quite different.

Even if species and ecosystems had value in themselves, that would only block helping animals if that value were a trump, beating any other consideration. If it is only a greater weight, large gains for animals can outweigh small environmental losses. And even as a trump, forms of help that don't affect environmental goals would still be permitted (Cunha, pp. 179–180).

text.bold: 9. If values add up, reducing suffering also raises the total.

paragraph.text: Whoever says that an ecosystem's beauty or richness makes up for the suffering in it is adding the two together. But, in that sum, reducing suffering without touching the ecosystem raises the total. The sum can't be used to refuse help (Cunha, pp. 180–182).

text.bold: 10. The same limit that already applies to humans.

paragraph.text: Those who defend conservation already limit it by the basic interests of human beings: no one accepts letting people die to protect a species or a landscape. Once speciesism is rejected, the same limit applies to other animals (Cunha, pp. 182–183).

text.bold: 11. Consistent biocentrism would call for more intervention, not less.

paragraph.text: If every living organism has a good of its own that matters, and population dynamics make most living beings die early, those who think this way would have reasons to help even more beings than the sentientist does. Cunha notes that authors such as Paul Taylor, who exclude domesticated animals, end up closer to naturocentrism than to biocentrism (pp. 184–185).

text.bold: 12. Ecology describes; it doesn't tell us what to do.

paragraph.text: When the philosopher Jeff McMahan argued for helping wild animals in

in 2010, the ecologist Paul Falkowski commented that he was treating a question of biology as one of ethics. Cunha calls this the "domain error": ecology describes the interactions among living things, and doesn't prescribe which of them should continue. Saying one shouldn't intervene is also a moral judgment (pp. 186–188). Ecology is a science; environmentalism is an ethical position, and the two shouldn't be confused.

text.bold: 13. Two examples of the conflict over method.

paragraph.text: In Europe, the North American ruddy duck, introduced to Britain in the 1940s, began interbreeding with the white-headed duck, an endangered species in Spain; since then, culling programmes have cut the European population of the American species to less than 7% of its 2000 level, in the name of the native species' "purity". The two birds play practically the same ecological role, and Catia Faria (2011) uses the case as an example of killing that serves no animal (Cunha, pp. 170–171). And so-called "sustainable" fishing preserves stocks, but each fish caught goes through the same suffering, by asphyxiation or decompression, as in overfishing (Mood, 2010; Cunha, p. 174).

text.bold: 14. For Singer, animal suffering is an argument for preservation.

paragraph.text: In

(ch. 10), Peter Singer, whose ethics gives intrinsic value only to the experiences of sentient beings, uses the example of a dam that would flood a valley. The animals living there don't peacefully move elsewhere: the wild isn't full of vacant niches waiting for occupants, and a territory able to support an animal is usually already taken. Most drown or starve, and that suffering, he says, shouldn't count for less than equivalent suffering in human beings. That weighs against the dam without any appeal to the intrinsic value of the ecosystem. He adds two more arguments: the duty to future generations, which the discount rate used by economists erases, since values a thousand years from now end up counting for almost nothing, and the aesthetic value of nature, which he compares to that of the paintings in the Louvre. A sentientist can, then, defend nature with strong reasons. The difference shows up in cases where preserving requires causing suffering (point 3).

(d) The strongest counter-reply: extinction is forever, and without biodiversity everything falls apart

The most serious version says: an extinct species doesn't come back. Ecosystems poor in species are more fragile, and their collapse harms all beings, sentient ones included. Faced with an irreversible loss, it's prudent to treat biodiversity as if it were untouchable. Besides, there are sentientist philosophers, such as Catia Faria and Eze Paez, who hold that animal ethics and environmental ethics are incompatible in their foundations.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
Preserving because collapse would harm those who feel is exactly the reason the sentientist accepts. The counter-reply confirms the position it set out to refute.

Irreversibility calls for caution and also for looking for means that don't kill: contraception, fences, relocation, habitat protection. The question "is there another way?" is the one we would ask if the ones affected were human.

text.bold: Different foundations aren't opposition on everything.

paragraph.text: Faria and Paez discuss what has value in itself. Saying that the two ethics start from different points isn't being against every conservation measure, still less hoping for extinctions. In practice, the two often agree.

11. What the argument gets right

It's right that sentientism and part of environmental ethics start from different values, and that this difference has practical consequences: there are conservation programs a sentientist doesn't support. It's also right that some sentientist texts treat biodiversity coldly, as if it were irrelevant, and that this grates on people who have devoted their lives to protecting habitats. The loss of species is a real problem, and extinction can't be undone.

But disagreeing with some methods isn't being against the goal. The sentientist wants forests standing, rivers clean and habitats protected whenever that is good for those who live in them, and it almost always is. What the sentientist refuses is the idea that an abstraction can be worth more than the beings who feel.
